subject: Mass Media / Mass Communication (Code: 318)
past_paper_reference: CUET UG Mass Media Past Papers (2022-2024)

questions.sub_topic: Public Communication Definition
questions.question: A communication setting where a single speaker delivers a prepared message or address to a large physically present audience (such as a lecture hall or political rally) is:
options: A) Public communication
B) Intrapersonal communication
C) Dyadic communication
D) Mass communication
questions.explanation: Public communication involves one person addressing a gathered audience in a structured setting with limited immediate verbal dialogue.

questions.sub_topic: Proxemics: Edward T. Hall's Spatial Zones
questions.question: In Edward T. Hall's proxemic theory, what distance defines the 'Social Distance' zone (typically observed in professional business meetings and casual social acquaintances)?
options: A) 0 to 18 inches
B) 4 to 12 feet
C) 1.5 to 4 feet
D) 12 to 25 feet and beyond
questions.explanation: Hall's 4 spatial zones: Intimate (0-18 in), Personal (1.5-4 ft), Social (4-12 ft), and Public (12-25+ ft).

questions.sub_topic: Osgood-Schramm Circular Model (1954)
questions.question: How did the Osgood-Schramm Model (1954) fundamentally revolutionize communication theory away from Shannon and Weaver's linear paradigm?
options: A) It eliminated all human communicators and replaced them with automated telegraph transmitters
B) It proved that communication can only travel along one-way copper telephone lines
C) It portrayed communication as an endless circular and reciprocal process where both participants perform identical functions: Encoding, Decoding, and Interpreting simultaneously
D) It stated that feedback only occurs if a written letter is mailed through the postal service
questions.explanation: Osgood-Schramm introduced circularity and reciprocity: communicators alternate continuously as encoders, decoders, and interpreters of shared meaning.

questions.sub_topic: Uses and Gratifications Theory: Katz, Blumler, and Gurevitch (1974)
questions.question: What paradigm-shifting question did the 'Uses and Gratifications' approach introduce to mass communication research in 1974?
options: A) Instead of asking 'Who owns the newspaper?', it asked 'How fast does the printing press spin?'
B) Instead of asking 'Why do people vote?', it asked 'Which political candidate spends the most money?'
C) Instead of asking 'What is news?', it asked 'How much does television broadcast equipment cost?'
D) Instead of asking 'What does media do to people?', it asked 'What do active people do with media?'
questions.explanation: Elihu Katz, Jay Blumler, and Michael Gurevitch flipped media effects research by treating audience members as goal-directed, active consumers seeking specific psychological gratifications.

questions.sub_topic: Cultivation Theory: Mainstreaming and Resonance
questions.question: In George Gerbner's cultivation theory, what occurs during the psychological process of 'Resonance'?
options: A) When viewers' real-world daily life experiences mirror what they repeatedly see depicted on television, giving the televised message a potent double-dose that magnifies cultivation effects
B) When television audio speakers vibrate violently during live musical broadcasts
C) When viewers turn off their television sets to read printed literary novels
D) When television channels broadcast in high-definition stereo frequencies
questions.explanation: Resonance occurs when an everyday real-world reality resembles televised portrayals (e.g., high-crime neighborhood resident watching crime drama), intensifying cultivation impact.

questions.sub_topic: Charles Sanders Peirce: Triadic Sign Model
questions.question: In Charles Sanders Peirce's triadic model of semiotics, which three interconnected elements constitute the generation of meaning (semiosis)?
options: A) The Signifier, the Signified, and the Linguistic Lexicon
B) The Representamen (Sign-vehicle), the Object (Referent), and the Interpretant (Mental effect or conception generated in the mind)
C) The Channel, the Noise, and the Transmitter
D) The Sender, the Message, and the Receiver
questions.explanation: Peirce's semiotic triad consists of the Representamen (the sign itself), the Object (what it references), and the Interpretant (the cognitive meaning created in the observer's mind).

questions.sub_topic: Robert McChesney: Media Conglomeration and Democracy (1999)
questions.question: In 'Rich Media, Poor Democracy' (1999), political economist Robert McChesney argues that oligopolistic hyper-commercial media consolidation subverts democratic governance because:
options: A) Television transmitters consume more electrical energy than national power grids can supply
B) Printed newspapers refuse to publish reports on sports and cultural entertainment

C) A handful of transnational corporate conglomerates prioritize advertising revenue and shareholder profit, gutting costly investigative journalism and replacing civic debate with superficial infotainment
D) Corporate conglomerates are legally prohibited from owning digital computer servers
questions.explanation: McChesney demonstrates that hyper-commercial corporate ownership deprives democracy of critical investigative journalism, creating an anemic civic sphere ruled by corporate profit motives.

questions.sub_topic: Jump Line in Newspaper Layout
questions.question: In newspaper layout, the brief directional text at the bottom of a front-page article indicating the page where the story continues (e.g., 'Continued on Page 4') is a:
options: A) Byline
B) Dateline
C) Cutline
D) Jump line
questions.explanation: A jump line directs the reader to the continuation (jump) page where the remainder of a front-page story is printed.

questions.sub_topic: Off-the-Record Rule in Journalism
questions.question: When an interviewee provides information to a reporter strictly 'Off-the-Record', what is the binding ethical rule regarding that information?
options: A) The information is for the reporter's personal background understanding only and cannot be published, quoted, or attributed in any form
B) The information must be published immediately on the newspaper's front page with full attribution
C) The reporter must record the interview on video and upload it to social media within an hour
D) The information can be published as long as the reporter spells the source's name backwards
questions.explanation: 'Off-the-record' means information cannot be published or quoted in any form; it serves purely to guide the reporter's understanding and prompt independent verification.

questions.sub_topic: Copy Editing Symbols and Workflow
questions.question: What is the primary editorial objective of a 'Copy Editor' (Sub-Editor) seated at the news desk before a reporter's draft goes to print?
options: A) To negotiate commercial advertising contract rates with corporate department stores
B) To verify factual accuracy, eliminate grammatical and spelling errors, ensure adherence to the publication's house style, check for libel, and write clear headlines
C) To physically operate the mechanical rotary printing presses in the basement factory
D) To physically deliver printed newspapers to suburban residential doorsteps
questions.explanation: Copy editors are the quality gatekeepers: checking facts, tightening prose, correcting grammar, applying stylebook consistency, catching legal libel, and writing headlines.

questions.sub_topic: Conflict and Human Interest News Values
questions.question: Why do parliamentary debates, court trials, and labor strikes receive consistently heavy news coverage under classical journalistic news values?
options: A) Because parliamentary debates are legally required to be printed on front pages by law
B) Because court trials are funded by corporate commercial advertising agencies
C) Because 'Conflict' is a primary news value: struggles between opposing forces, ideologies, or institutions contain inherent dramatic tension and high public stakes
D) Because labor strikes are the only events that printing press machines can legally report
questions.explanation: Conflict—clashes between institutions, values, or political factions—possesses high intrinsic dramatic tension, driving public interest and accountability.

questions.sub_topic: Raja Ram Mohan Roy: Sambad Kaumudi (1821) and Mirat-ul-Akhbar (1822)
questions.question: Why is Raja Ram Mohan Roy celebrated as the 'Father of Indian Language Journalism'?
options: A) He established the first computerized digital television station in Calcutta
B) He was the British Governor-General who imposed the first printing press licensing laws
C) He imported the first steam-powered rotary printing press from Germany to Bombay

D) He pioneered indigenous vernacular journalism by founding 'Sambad Kaumudi' in Bengali (1821) and 'Mirat-ul-Akhbar' in Persian (1822) to advocate social reform, abolish Sati, and champion free speech
questions.explanation: Ram Mohan Roy pioneered socio-political reform journalism in regional languages, using Sambad Kaumudi and Mirat-ul-Akhbar to campaign against Sati and colonial press ordinances.

questions.sub_topic: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1973): Newsprint Policy
questions.question: In the landmark Supreme Court ruling 'Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India' (1973), why was the government's Import Policy for Newsprint (fixing 10-page ceiling on major dailies) struck down?
options: A) Directly regulating page ceilings and newsprint quotas under the guise of rationing raw materials was an unconstitutional abridgment of the freedom of the press and circulation under Article 19(1)(a)
B) The newsprint policy was enacted without the written consent of foreign paper manufacturers
C) The Bennett Coleman publishing group had failed to pay corporate income tax duties
D) Newsprint paper was found to contain hazardous chemical dyes that damaged printing presses
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court ruled that controlling page limits under newsprint rationing was an indirect method of throttling press freedom and circulation, violating Article 19(1)(a).

questions.sub_topic: Watergate Scandal: Sourcing and Corroboration Standard
questions.question: During their historic Watergate investigation for The Washington Post, what rigorous corroboration rule did editor Ben Bradlee mandate for reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein before publishing any damaging allegation?
options: A) Every fact had to be personally approved by the President of the United States in writing
B) Every critical fact or allegation had to be independently confirmed by at least two separate, reliable sources
C) Allegations could only be published if verified by polygraph lie detector tests
D) Reporters were required to wait ten years before publishing any investigative scoop
questions.explanation: Ben Bradlee enforced the famous 'two-source rule': no accusation could run without independent corroboration from two distinct, verified sources.

questions.sub_topic: Logo and Brand Identity Definition
questions.question: A unique graphic mark, emblem, or stylized symbol used by an organization to identify its brand, products, and services across marketing touchpoints is a:
options: A) Slug
B) Cutline
C) Logo (or Brand Mark)
D) Byline
questions.explanation: A logo is the core visual anchor of brand identity, fostering instant public recognition across packaging, advertisements, and digital media.

questions.sub_topic: Comparative Advertising Legal Guidelines
questions.question: Under trade law and ASCI guidelines in India, when is an advertiser permitted to use 'Comparative Advertising' mentioning a rival competitor's product?
options: A) Only when the rival brand's chief executive officer gives written permission in an affidavit
B) Only during political election campaigns between registered legislative candidates
C) Comparative advertising is completely and unconditionally banned under all circumstances in India
D) When the comparison is based on clear, factual, and substantiated claims comparing identical features, without disparaging, denigrating, or defaming the competitor's trademark
questions.explanation: Comparative advertising is permissible if comparisons are truthful, relevant, and verifiable, but advertisers cannot unfairly denigrate or disparage rival products.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Press Communique vs Press Release
questions.question: In official government communications, what distinguishes a 'Press Communiqué' from a routine press release?
options: A) A Press Communiqué is a formal, authoritative official declaration issued on matters of high state importance (such as ministerial appointments or treaty pacts) that newspapers are expected to carry verbatim
B) A Press Communiqué is a secret document that is never shown to journalists or the public
C) A Press Communiqué is printed exclusively on handmade cotton rag paper in calligraphy
D) A Press Communiqué is a commercial advertising contract purchased from private agencies
questions.explanation: A Press Communiqué carries official sovereign weight on major state developments (cabinet reshuffles, policy declarations) intended to be published in full without editorial trimming.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Advertising Media
questions.sub_topic: Target Rating Points (TRP) Calculation in Broadcast
questions.question: In television broadcast advertising, what do 'Target Rating Points' (TRPs) measure compared to generic Gross Rating Points (GRPs)?
options: A) TRPs measure the physical weight of television antennas installed in suburban homes
B) TRPs measure the percentage of the specific target demographic audience (e.g., women aged 18-34) reached by a commercial, whereas GRPs measure the gross total audience universe
C) TRPs calculate the total number of words spoken in a thirty-second commercial script
D) TRPs measure the speed of electromagnetic radio waves traveling through the atmosphere
questions.explanation: While GRP measures gross reach across all households, TRP isolates reach and frequency specifically within the defined target consumer demographic.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Crisis PR: Tylenol Tampering Case Study (Johnson & Johnson, 1982)
questions.question: Why is Johnson & Johnson's response to the 1982 Chicago Tylenol cyanide poisoning crisis celebrated in business history as the gold standard of ethical crisis PR?
options: A) The company denied all responsibility, blamed the victims, and sued local newspaper journalists
B) The company concealed the deaths from public health regulators for over six months

C) CEO James Burke prioritized consumer safety over short-term profits by immediately recalling 31 million bottles nationwide, cooperating fully with media and FBI, and pioneering tamper-evident triple packaging
D) The company permanently shut down all operations and dissolved the corporate organization
questions.explanation: J&J's swift, transparent response—immediate national recall, open media engagement, and inventing tamper-evident packaging—restored consumer trust and saved the brand.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Advertising Theory
questions.sub_topic: Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986)
questions.question: In Richard Petty and John Cacioppo's Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) of persuasion, which route to persuasion produces enduring, attitude change resistant to counter-persuasion?
options: A) The Peripheral Route—where consumers rely on superficial heuristics like celebrity attractiveness
B) The Subliminal Route—where messages are hidden beneath conscious perceptual thresholds
C) The Autonomous Route—where computers make automated purchasing decisions for humans
D) The Central Route—where motivated and able consumers actively scrutinize, process, and elaborate on the rational arguments and factual evidence presented in the message
questions.explanation: ELM posits Central Route processing (deep cognitive elaboration of message arguments) yields durable, counter-attitudinally resistant beliefs, whereas Peripheral Route cues yield fleeting changes.

questions.sub_topic: Extreme Close-Up (ECU) Shot Psychological Effect
questions.question: A camera shot that magnifies a single isolated facial feature—such as a character's twitching eye or trembling mouth—filling the entire screen with dramatic intensity is an:
options: A) Extreme Close-Up (ECU / XCU)
B) Extreme Long Shot (ELS)
C) Medium Shot (MS)
D) Establishing Shot
questions.explanation: An Extreme Close-Up (ECU) isolates a minute detail or feature, magnifying intense emotional focus and dramatic intimacy.

questions.sub_topic: Gels / Color Gels in Studio Lighting
questions.question: Heat-resistant transparent colored plastic sheets placed in front of studio lighting fixtures to tint the illumination with specific colors or correct color temperature are called:
options: A) Barn doors
B) Color gels
C) Snoots
D) Gobos
questions.explanation: Color gels (or lighting filters) alter the color output of studio lights for dramatic mood or color temperature conversion (e.g., CTB/CTO gels).

questions.sub_topic: Cutaway Shot in Television Editing
questions.question: In television news editing, what is the functional purpose of inserting a 'Cutaway' shot (such as a shot of an interviewer nodding or a clock on the wall)?
options: A) To permanently delete the sound recording from the video camera's digital memory
B) To indicate that the television program has officially concluded and roll closing credits
C) To cover a jump cut or audio splice in the main interview footage, bridging discontinuous edits smoothly without disorienting the viewer
D) To test whether the television transmitter is broadcasting at the correct frequency
questions.explanation: A cutaway cuts away from main action to a related visual element (e.g., interviewer nodding, B-roll), seamlessly masking dialogue edits and jump cuts.

questions.sub_topic: Depth of Field: Shallow vs Deep Depth of Field
questions.question: In television camera optics, how does 'Shallow Depth of Field' isolate a subject visually within the frame?
options: A) The entire frame from inches in front of the lens to the distant horizon is in sharp focus
B) The camera sensor converts all color tones into pure black-and-white silhouettes
C) The video image is projected in reverse order from the bottom of the screen to the top
D) Only the main subject remains in sharp optical focus, while the foreground and background are softly blurred out (bokeh), directing viewer attention directly to the subject
questions.explanation: Shallow depth of field uses wide apertures (low f-stop) or long focal lengths to keep the subject crisp while blurring the background, isolating focal interest.

questions.sub_topic: Role of the Teleprompter Operator
questions.question: During a live news broadcast, what must a 'Teleprompter Operator' continuously do to ensure seamless on-air delivery by the news anchor?
options: A) Match the scrolling speed of the script on the glass display in real time to the anchor's natural reading cadence and spontaneous pauses
B) Physically clean the television camera lenses using specialized chemical spray solutions
C) Operate the sound mixing console to ensure commercial advertisements play at high volume
D) Write the daily editorial opinion columns for morning print newspapers
questions.explanation: A prompter operator rides the scroll speed to pace the anchor's natural speech, pausing when the anchor ad-libs and tracking vocal cadence.

questions.sub_topic: 180-Degree Rule in Multi-Camera Continuity
questions.question: In multi-camera television drama, what spatial disorientation occurs if a camera crosses the imaginary '180-Degree Line' (Axis of Action)?
options: A) The television studio lighting fixtures immediately overheat and shut down
B) The left-right screen direction of characters reverses abruptly, causing conversational partners who were looking at each other to appear to look in the same direction, disorienting the viewer
C) The audio soundtrack is played in reverse audio from finish to start
D) The video resolution drops from high-definition 1080p to low-definition 240p
questions.explanation: Crossing the 180-degree axis inverts screen direction, making characters who were facing each other appear to gaze in the same direction, violating spatial continuity.

questions.sub_topic: Loudness Measurement Unit (Decibel)
questions.question: In audio physics and sound recording, the physical intensity, volume, or sound pressure level of an acoustic signal is measured in:
options: A) Hertz (Hz)
B) Lumens (lm)
C) Decibels (dB)
D) Kelvin (K)
questions.explanation: The Decibel (dB) is the logarithmic unit expressing the ratio of physical sound pressure to the threshold of human hearing.

questions.sub_topic: Cardioid Polar Pattern Shape and Rejection
questions.question: Why is a 'Cardioid' microphone pickup pattern universally preferred for vocal recording in broadcast radio studios?
options: A) It captures sound equally from all directions in a three-hundred-sixty-degree circle
B) It captures sound exclusively from the sides while completely muting the front
C) It converts spoken human words into written text on computer monitor screens
D) Its heart-shaped pattern is most sensitive to sound arriving from the front while rejecting sound from the rear (180°), isolating the presenter's voice from ambient studio reflections
questions.explanation: Cardioid (heart-shaped) microphones pick up sound from the front while exhibiting maximum rejection at the rear (180°), preventing spill and feedback.

questions.sub_topic: Acoustic Cue / Stinger in Radio Packaging
questions.question: In radio broadcasting, what is an audio 'Stinger' (or Sound Stager)?
options: A) A brief, punchy musical chord or dramatic sound effect (lasting 1-3 seconds) used to punctuate an important announcement, transition between topics, or emphasize a news headline
B) A technical electrical shock delivered to the audio engineer's headphones
C) A sixty-minute uninterrupted classical musical symphony broadcast without commentary
D) A written legal contract signed between the radio presenter and the station owner
questions.explanation: A stinger is a crisp, punchy audio burst or musical stab used to punctuate transitions, introduce segments, or emphasize key statements in radio packaging.

questions.sub_topic: AIR Motto: Bahujana Hitaya Bahujana Sukhaya (1956)
questions.question: Adopted in 1956, what is the official Sanskrit motto of All India Radio (AIR), and what philosophy does it embody?
options: A) 'Satyameva Jayate' ('Truth Alone Triumphs')
B) 'Bahujana Hitaya Bahujana Sukhaya' ('For the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many'), reflecting its public service mandate to serve the entire diverse nation
C) 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' ('The World is One Family')
D) 'Yogakshemam Vahamyaham' ('I shall provide what they need')
questions.explanation: All India Radio adopted the Rigvedic motto 'Bahujana Hitaya Bahujana Sukhaya' in 1956, affirming its public service commitment to national education, culture, and progress.

questions.sub_topic: Balanced vs Unbalanced Audio Cables (XLR vs RCA/TS)
questions.question: In professional broadcast sound studios, why are 'Balanced Audio Cables' (using three-pin XLR connectors) universally mandated over unbalanced cables?
options: A) Balanced cables can only transmit sound waves if the sound engineer is wearing rubber boots
B) Balanced cables eliminate the need for microphones by recording sound directly from the air
C) They carry two copies of the audio signal (hot and cold in opposite polarity); when the receiver flips the inverted signal, common-mode electromagnetic noise and hum are completely cancelled out
D) Balanced cables are legally required to be painted bright orange by broadcasting safety laws
questions.explanation: Balanced lines use Common-Mode Rejection (CMR): two out-of-phase signal lines (+ and -) and a ground shield cancel out induced electromagnetic interference at the differential receiver.

questions.sub_topic: Orson Welles: The War of the Worlds Panic Broadcast (1938)
questions.question: Why did Orson Welles' Mercury Theatre radio broadcast of 'The War of the Worlds' on October 30, 1938 cause panic among thousands of American listeners?
options: A) Actual Martian spacecraft physically landed in suburban New Jersey during the broadcast
B) The radio station transmitter emitted high-frequency ultrasonic waves that frightened listeners
C) The broadcast was officially sanctioned by the US President as a real national emergency alert
D) It adapted H.G. Wells' sci-fi novel as a series of realistic, breaking news bulletin interruptions and eyewitness actualities, exploiting the audience's deep trust in the radio medium
questions.explanation: Welles pioneered radio docudrama: formatting the alien invasion as breaking news bulletins interrupting dance music, exploiting listeners' conditioned faith in radio news authority.

questions.sub_topic: Bird's Eye View / Overhead Shot Function
questions.question: A camera shot captured from directly above the subject looking straight down (as if from the sky or ceiling) is an:
options: A) Overhead shot (or Bird's-Eye View / Top Shot)
B) Low-Angle shot
C) Close-Up shot
D) Dutch Angle shot
questions.explanation: An overhead (bird's-eye) shot looks straight down from 90 degrees, offering a detached, geometric, or omniscient godlike perspective on characters and terrain.

questions.sub_topic: Soviet Montage Theory: Lev Kuleshov Effect
questions.question: In the famous 1920s Kuleshov Experiment, filmmaker Lev Kuleshov demonstrated that cinema is defined by editing by proving that:
options: A) Audiences refused to watch movies that were projected at twenty-four frames per second
B) Viewers derived different emotional meanings from the exact same actor's expression depending on whether it was juxtaposed with a bowl of soup, a dead woman, or a playing child
C) Actors who spoke loudly into microphones were perceived as five feet taller by audiences
D) Motion pictures could only be understood if projected on red velvet curtains
questions.explanation: The Kuleshov effect proved editing creates psychological meaning: juxtaposing the same impassive face of Mozzhukhin with soup, a coffin, or a child sparked hunger, grief, or affection.

questions.sub_topic: Indian Parallel Cinema: Adoor Gopalakrishnan (Swayamvaram, 1972)
questions.question: Which visionary Malayalam filmmaker debuted with 'Swayamvaram' (1972)—funded by the Film Finance Corporation—inaugurating the New Cinema movement in Kerala?
options: A) G. Aravindan
B) John Abraham
C) Adoor Gopalakrishnan
D) P. Padmarajan
questions.explanation: Adoor Gopalakrishnan's 'Swayamvaram' (1972) won four National Awards, pioneering serious New Wave realism in Malayalam cinema through its austere aesthetic and psychological depth.

questions.sub_topic: Diegetic vs Non-Diegetic Sound Distinction
questions.question: In film audio analysis, what is the difference between 'Diegetic Sound' and 'Non-Diegetic Sound'?
options: A) Diegetic sound is recorded in space, while non-diegetic sound is recorded underwater
B) Diegetic sound is silent, while non-diegetic sound is very loud
C) Diegetic sound is heard only by the audience, while non-diegetic sound is heard by characters

D) Diegetic sound exists within the fictional world of the film and can be heard by the characters (dialogue, car horn); Non-Diegetic sound originates outside the story world (dramatic musical score, voiceover)
questions.explanation: Diegetic sound has its source in the story world (audible to characters); non-diegetic sound exists outside the narrative reality (orchestral score, external narrator).

questions.sub_topic: Siegfried Kracauer: Theory of Film - The Redemption of Physical Reality (1960)
questions.question: In his realist cinema treatise 'Theory of Film: The Redemption of Physical Reality' (1960), Siegfried Kracauer argued that the fundamental photographic affinity of cinema is to:
options: A) Record and reveal transient, indeterminate physical reality—the flow of real life, inanimate objects, and accidental occurrences—rescuing the physical world from oblivion
B) Construct artificial theatrical fantasy illusions using painted studio sets and costumes
C) Convert motion picture celluloid film into written literary novels for university libraries
D) Demonstrate how computer software algorithms can replace all human motion picture actors
questions.explanation: Kracauer argued cinema's unique mission is the 'redemption of physical reality': capturing the unstageable, transient, material textures of real life that other arts cannot record.

questions.sub_topic: Cinematograph Act, 1952: Section 5B Constitutional Guidelines
questions.question: Under Section 5B(1) of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 in India, on what specific grounds can the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) deny certification to a film?
options: A) If the film's production budget was financed with foreign currency funds

B) If the film is against the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency, or involves defamation/contempt of court
C) If the director of the film did not graduate from the Film and Television Institute of India
D) If the film lasts longer than one hundred twenty minutes in total running duration
questions.explanation: Section 5B(1) directly mirrors the reasonable restrictions of Article 19(2), establishing the statutory grounds on which the CBFC can refuse certification or order cuts.

questions.sub_topic: Podcast Hosting Platforms Function
questions.question: A digital service (such as Libsyn, Spotify for Podcasters, or Podbean) that stores audio files and generates public RSS feeds for podcast distribution is a:
options: A) Video switcher
B) Teleprompter
C) Podcast host (or Podcast hosting platform)
D) Chroma keyer
questions.explanation: Podcast hosting services store large media files (MP3s) and manage the RSS feed that syndicates audio episodes to directories and podcast apps.

questions.sub_topic: Phishing vs Catfishing on Social Media
questions.question: In social media culture, the deceptive practice where an individual creates a fake online identity, profile, and photographs to deceive someone into an emotional romantic relationship is:
options: A) Blogging
B) Vlogging
C) Podcasting
D) Catfishing
questions.explanation: Catfishing involves constructing a fabricated social media identity to lure someone into a relationship or manipulate them under false pretenses.

questions.sub_topic: Filter Bubble: Eli Pariser Formulation (2011)
questions.question: In his influential book 'The Filter Bubble' (2011), Eli Pariser warned that personalized internet search and news algorithms create an intellectual trap by:
options: A) Automatically isolating users in their own unique cultural and ideological bubble based on their past click history, silently editing out contrasting viewpoints
B) Physically filtering out dust and dirt particles from computer cooling fans
C) Forcing all internet websites to display text in a single font size and color
D) Permanently deleting all user account passwords after thirty days of inactivity
questions.explanation: Eli Pariser showed that personalized algorithms construct an invisible 'filter bubble' that feeds users confirming biases while filtering out uncongenial information.

questions.sub_topic: Influencer Sponsored Content Disclosures (ASCI Guidelines)
questions.question: Under the Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) Guidelines for Influencer Advertising, what prominent disclosure must social media influencers make when promoting a paid product?
options: A) They must state that they personally manufactured the product in their own home kitchen
B) They must clearly display prominent disclosure labels (such as #Ad, #Sponsored, or #Collab) in the post and video, ensuring consumers know it is commercial promotional content
C) They must provide a complete refund of the retail purchase price to all social media followers
D) They are legally barred from uploading photographs of the product packaging on mobile apps
questions.explanation: ASCI mandates upfront, clear, unmissable disclosure tags (#Ad, #Sponsored, #Partnership) on influencer posts so consumers distinguish paid promotions from authentic personal reviews.

questions.sub_topic: Bernard Stiegler: Hyper-Industrialization and Attention Capture
questions.question: In his philosophical critique of digital capitalism, French philosopher Bernard Stiegler argued that contemporary psychotechnology and social media networks destroy human culture through:
options: A) The physical replacement of mechanical automobile assembly robots with human labor
B) The legal ban on digital social networking platforms enacted by international treaties
C) The industrial capture and short-circuiting of deep attention, replacing transgenerational knowledge and maturity with impulsive, addictive short-term consumption
D) The permanent destruction of electromagnetic radio transmission antennas by lightning storms
questions.explanation: Stiegler warned that digital media captures human attentional mechanisms, eroding long-term focus, transgenerational transmission of knowledge, and cultural sublimation.

questions.sub_topic: Context Collapse in Networked Publics (Michael Wesch / danah boyd)
questions.question: In digital social media sociology, what sociolinguistic crisis is captured by the concept of 'Context Collapse'?
options: A) The physical collapse of digital computer server racks in telecommunications data centers
B) A software bug that causes social media smartphone applications to delete text messages
C) The legal dissolution of social media companies ordered by national supreme courts
D) The flattening of multiple distinct, separate social audiences (family, colleagues, close friends, employers) into a single homogenous online audience on a platform profile
questions.explanation: Context collapse occurs when disparate social worlds collide on a single feed, forcing users to navigate conflicting social expectations without contextual boundaries.

questions.sub_topic: Internet Protocol (IP) Address Definition
questions.question: A unique numerical identifier assigned to every device connected to a computer network that uses the Internet Protocol for communication (such as 192.168.1.1) is an:
options: A) IP address (Internet Protocol address)
B) HTML tag
C) Byline
D) ISBN number
questions.explanation: An IP address uniquely identifies each device on a network, enabling data packets to be routed accurately across the global internet.

questions.sub_topic: Cloud Computing Definition
questions.question: The on-demand delivery of computing services—including data storage, servers, databases, and software—over the internet rather than on a local computer hard drive is:
options: A) Broadcast television
B) Cloud computing
C) Rotary printing
D) Direct mailing
questions.explanation: Cloud computing delivers scalable computing resources (servers, storage, software) over the internet on-demand, eliminating local infrastructure overhead.

questions.sub_topic: Citizen Journalism Characteristics
questions.question: What is 'Citizen Journalism', and how has the proliferation of smartphones and social media empowered it?
options: A) Journalists who work exclusively for municipal government state departments
B) A specialized legal court that prosecutes journalists who make factual reporting errors
C) Ordinary citizens playing an active role in collecting, reporting, analyzing, and disseminating news and breaking eyewitness footage without professional journalistic training
D) A system where citizens are legally required to purchase ten newspapers every morning
questions.explanation: Citizen journalism involves non-professionals capturing and publishing firsthand accounts, photos, and videos of breaking news, democratizing information flows.

questions.sub_topic: Henry Jenkins: Transmedia Storytelling Definition (2006)
questions.question: In media convergence theory, what defines 'Transmedia Storytelling' (as formulated by Henry Jenkins in 'Convergence Culture')?
options: A) Publishing the exact same motion picture script as a paperback book without changing a single word
B) Broadcasting a television show on two different channels simultaneously at the same hour
C) Translating an English newspaper article into three regional vernacular languages
D) A narrative that unfolds across multiple media platforms, with each distinct medium (film, novel, video game, social media) making a unique, valuable contribution to the larger story world
questions.explanation: Transmedia storytelling disperses narrative elements systematically across multiple platforms (film, comics, web, games), with each platform doing what it does best to deepen immersion.

questions.sub_topic: Alexander Galloway and Eugene Thacker: The Exploit (Protocol and Power)
questions.question: In 'The Exploit: A Theory of Networks' (2007), Alexander Galloway and Eugene Thacker argue that political resistance in networked protocol societies must take the form of:
options: A) An 'Exploit'—finding and leveraging the inherent structural vulnerabilities, asymmetries, and holes within the network's own protocols and algorithmic logic to disrupt power from within
B) Building armed wooden sailing ships to engage in maritime warfare on international oceans
C) Physically cutting down telephone poles with axes to disconnect electric wires
D) Writing handwritten letters to monarchical rulers demanding the abolition of machines
questions.explanation: Galloway and Thacker assert that in protocol-governed networks, resistance cannot operate through traditional exterior opposition; it must discover the 'exploit' immanent in the network rules.

questions.sub_topic: Jaron Lanier: You Are Not a Gadget (2010) Cybernetic Totalism
questions.question: In his foundational digital manifesto 'You Are Not a Gadget' (2010), virtual reality pioneer Jaron Lanier critiques Web 2.0 social platforms for promoting 'Cybernetic Totalism', which:
options: A) Forces every software programmer to wear three-dimensional virtual reality helmets continuously
B) Abolishes all commercial manufacturing of silicon computer microprocessors
C) Requires internet users to donate fifty percent of their income to public software foundations
D) Degrades individual human creativity and personhood into crowd wisdom and atomized database entries, designing humans to be components of a hive-mind software machine
questions.explanation: Lanier critiques the reduction of human uniqueness to algorithmically aggregated crowd data ('the hive mind'), arguing digital platforms design humans to fit software templates.
